div.p: Real-time multimedia applications willl require guaranteed quality of service (QoS) such as a bound on the maximum message delay and/or on the maximum message loss rate. This poses an exciting challenge to the highspeed transport protocol design and implementations. In this paper, we study the resource and connection admission control algorithms, and give the neclessary and sufficient conditions for the schedulability, of n real-time transport connections at a destination host under preemptive and non-preemptive deadline schedluling policy for deterministic QoS guarantees. These necessary and sufficient condition? form the mathematical basis for the deterministic QoS guarantees in real-time transport communication services. On the basis of these necessary and sufficient conditions, we give the connection admission control algorithms for deterministic QoS guarantees. We also calculate the buffer space needed for each real-time transport connection. The results show that real-time transport connections with deterministic QoS guarantees can reserve the buffer space at the establishment phase, and no flow control mechanism is required during the data transport phase. Our results could be applied to other fields as well, such as real-time operating systems.

div.head: Introduction to the quality of transport service
div.p: In the OS1 transport service definition [l], the term Quality of Service (QoS) refers to certain characteristics of a transport service as observed by the transport service users. The transport layer is requiredl to provide the QoS parameters with the best effort and at minimum cost. The OS1 8072 connection-mode transport service definition associates with each transport connection at its time of establishment the opportunity to request, negotiate and have agreed a certain set of QoS parameters by the transport service provider. The OS1 80172 connection-mode compulsory QoS. If a compulsory QoS is not satisfied after its negotiation, the transport service provider must reject the connection request; c). threshold QoS. After its negotiation the transport provider will have to monitor the transport connection and to issue a special indication primitive to the transport service users whenever it notices its inability to maintain the request threshold QoS values. Another high speed transport service is defined in [4], and its QoS parameters are defined in [5,6,71. The parameters specifying the traffic to be given by the client include parameters expressing peak and average load on the network, and an indication of bursthess of load. The QoS Parameters are (a). delay bound; (b). delay violation probability bound; (c). buffer overflow probability bound; and (d). delay jitter bound. All these parameters are allowed to take v<dues from a continuous range. XTP is a new high speed transport protocol [8], which has been enhanced to provide the QoS transport requirements in an internetwork environment of multimedia applications to control the access to the resources based on a contract between the user and the transport service provider [9]. The basic concept in XTP design is the notion of "real-time" or "flow-through'' processing. The idea is to pass data units through a pipeline of protocol engines. In short, the transport services and QoS parameters for real-time multimedia applications are the focus of wide researches in high speed networks such as ATM. High speed transport protocols which support real-time transport connections are referred to as real-time transport protocols.

Multimedia applications can be divided broadly into two classes, those with real-time constraints and those without. Traditional networking applications such as file transfer, electronic mail, and remote login do not have real-time constraints. The performance metrics of interest for these applications are typically the average packet delay and the throughput. Of more interest to us are those applications with real-time constraints. In the following section, we identify the classification of QoS requirements and formulate the problems to be considered. In order to let the terminology be identical, we use the "message" to represent the "transport protocol data unit" (TPDU) throughout this paper. Note that QoS requirements are typically specified on an end-to-end basis. This imposes requirements on the hosts at each end as well as the network connecting them. We will only focus on the host QoS requirements here (although our ideas could be extended to the network).

div.head: Problem statements
div.p: Future transport protocols must guarantee the QoS performance required by the transport service users. For non-real-time applications, the transport service provider will do its best to reach the QoS parameters required by the transport service users. Nothing will be done in case the transport service provider is unable to maintain the required QoS parameters. Real-time applications are characterized by a message delay bound D and a maximum message delay bound violation rate pr (i.e., the maximum message loss rate due to delay bound violation). We do not mention here the message loss rate due to buffer overflow, since we will give an efficient buffer allocation mechanism by which the buffer will never overflow. That is to say, buffer space for real-time communication at hosts is always available. Thus a deadline is associated with each message and, if a message reaches its destination after its deadline, it may be considered useless and discarded. Some real-time applications, such as distributed control processing, have a very strict QoS performance requirement, that is, the message must arrive at its destination before its deadline, and pr =O. We identify these QoS performance guarantees as deterministic QoS guarantees. Other real-time applications, such as voice and video, can tolerate some fractions of message loss (approximately -IO-* 1.

Here message losses occur as a result of message processing scheduling at hosts, hence pr >O. We identify these QoS performance guarantees as statistical QoS guarantees. To simplify our discussion, we will only consider the deterministic QoS guarantees here. This would allow us to postpone the treatment of the statistical QoS guarantees, which would make this paper appreciably longer, to a subsequent paper.

There have been some works on real-time connection admission control performed to include the deterministic QoS guarantees as a part of high speed transport protocols and their implementations. Some references that discuss these topics can be find in [15, 161. The difficulty is that high speed transport protocol implementation on a general protocol processor is controlled by the operating system, whereas the context switching among transport connections is controlled by the operating system scheduler. Most operating systems are too coarse to provide the desired QoS requirements for real-time applications [10,11].

Resource allocation among real-time transport connections at hosts in high speed transport protocols is a very important issue, and must be extensively investigated. If the host supports multiple real-time transport connections, the performance seen by the transport service users depends on the resources (protocol processor, buffer space) available to that connection. The fraction of processing time given to each real-time transport connection determines its QoS performance. In order to guarantee the QoS of each real-time transport connection, the source host must specify its message generation pattern at the connection establishment phase. Because of the limited capability of the protocol processor, no bounded message delivery delay can be guaranteed without this information. For our study in this area, we chose the following two parameters: minimum message interarrival time T, and maximum message processing time p . div.head: Deterministic QoS gmrantees under preemptive deadline scheduling policy
div.p: Deadline scheduling [ 121 is used for packet scheduling and admission control [6] under the assumption that the sum of the maximum packet transmission times over all real-time connections passing through a link is not larger than the minimum packet interarrival time of these connections. For our purpose in real-time transport connections, we do not impose this restriction, since this assumption is quite restrictive in practice (the traffic types to be served are limited). Under the preemptive deadline scheduling policy, a message with the earliest deadline is always processed first. When a new message with an earlier deadline arrives, the processing of the current message is preempted, and will be resumed later after all processing of messages with earlier deadlines are completed. The switching time from one message to another is assumed to be negligible.

div.head: Deterministic QoS guarantees under non-preemptive deadline scheduling
div.p: The feasibility equations in theorem 1, 2 and 3 are based on the assumption of preemptive deadline scheduling policy. Preemption, however, is of much more potential overhead than non-preemption. It is, therefore, very important to study the feasibility of non-preemptive deadline scheduling policy in real-time transport protocols.

With the non-preemptive deadline scheduling policy, a message with the earliest deadline is always processed fmt at scheduling points (the processor is idle), but the processing of a message in progress can not be preempted by another message that has an earlier deadline.
We derive solutions to problem 1, 2 and 3 under nonpreemptive deadline scheduling in this section.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: This study was undertaken to determine the feasibility of offering real-time services in transport communications. Real-time services are characterized by the QoS guarantees. Such guarantees in real-time transport protocols are achieved by two techniques: admission control via connection establishment procedures and scheduling of message processing. We defined the problems and the traffic types, focused our attention on deterministic QoS guarantees, derived solutions to the schedulability of realtime transport connections, and gave connection admission control algorithms under preemptive and non-preemptive deadline scheduling policy respectively; theorem 1 to theorem 6 give a mathematical basis for the deterministic QoS guarantees at the destination host. From our calculation of buffer space allocation, we can conclude that real-time transport connections with deterministic QoS guarantees both under preemptive deadline scheduling policy and non-preemptive deadline scheduling policy can at the establishment reserve the buffer space Bi= phase, and no flow control mechanism is required during the data transport phase.
Our results could be applied to both real-time operating systems that support multimedia applications, and network nodes with QoS guarantees.
